items.title: Google ships A2UI 1.0, an open protocol letting AI agents render native interactive screens
items.summary: A2UI gives agents a way to generate real interactive UI instead of a wall of text or a fragile screenshot: renderer SDKs ship for React, Angular, Lit, Flutter, SwiftUI, and Jetpack Compose, with agent-side SDKs in Python, TypeScript, and Dart. 1.0 adds bidirectional function calls (the UI can call back into the agent), swappable inference formats, and secure data binding so an agent can't silently rewrite fields it shouldn't touch.
items.why: Right now most agent UIs are either a chat transcript or a one-off hand-built component — this is Google's bet on a standard the two can share, with a React SDK on day one.
items.action: Pull the A2UI React SDK and have an agent render one real interactive form (not just text) for a task you already automate, to see how the bidirectional calls actually feel.

eval.reason: Genuine new open protocol + multi-platform SDK release dated Nov 11, 2026 (authors Vishal Motwani and the Google A2UI Team), not pricing/benchmark news. Checked against the full Drive run-log history (Nov 5-11) and the public repo's briefs; not a duplicate.
Re-fetched developers.googleblog.com/a2ui-10-build-delightful-fast-reliable-agentic-experiences/ live this run; resolves to the specific post, not a homepage or aggregator.

SDK list (React, Angular, Lit, Flutter, SwiftUI, Jetpack Compose; Python/TypeScript/Dart agent SDKs), bidirectional function calls, swappable inference formats, and secure data binding are all taken directly from the fetched post.

Genuinely searched. The post embeds two first-party Google-hosted MP4 clips (not YouTube) as illustrations, and the only YouTube walkthrough found is from a third-party channel (Soverius AI), correctly excluded per the first-party-only rule.
Directly relevant to Vikas's React/TypeScript stack and interest in agent tooling; concrete, testable via a real SDK, not a roadmap promise.

items.title: Anthropic ships Claude Whiteboards and Sheets (beta), and makes Claude Data generally available
items.summary: Claude Whiteboards turns a talked-through plan into a shared, editable board with timelines and owners; Claude Sheets builds real spreadsheets (tabs, formulas, 144 functions, up to 100,000 cells) from a prompt and exports to Excel; Claude Data (formerly Dashboards) is now GA, with certified metric badges, narrated video summaries, and dashboard caching. A related Interactive Connectors feature lets Adobe, Atlassian, HubSpot, and others open as full apps inside Claude.
items.why: If you've been exporting Claude's answers into a spreadsheet or a deck by hand, that step is now something Claude can just do, in place, with real edit history.
items.action: Ask Claude to turn a messy planning conversation into a Sheet with real formulas, or a Whiteboard with owners and dates, instead of a plain list.

eval.reason: Four genuinely new capabilities shipped Nov 10, 2026, distinct from the already-sent Claude Fable 5.2/Mythos 5.2 model release (Nov 9/10); not a duplicate of anything in the Drive log history.
Re-fetched claude.com/resources/articles/sheets-whiteboards-data live this run; resolves to the specific announcement, dated Nov 10, 2026.
Tool descriptions (Whiteboards beta, Sheets beta/144 functions/100k cells, Data GA formerly Dashboards, Interactive Connectors with named partners Adobe/Atlassian/HubSpot) match the re-fetched page.

Vikas uses Claude directly; these are concrete new capabilities with a verified first-party walkthrough, not vaporware.

items.title: Simon Willison puts Google's new Gemini Decisions API through its paces — the only one of the three that's truly multimodal
items.summary: Google joins OpenAI's GPT-6 Luna and the third-party Jev in the "decision model" category with Gemini Decision 1: instead of generating text token by token, it scores up to 1,000 yes/no, choice, or rubric questions against one input in a single pass, in 150-250ms, for $0.10/M input tokens with free output. Willison's own test fed it a video file alongside four yes/no questions (dragon? robot? set in France? set in the USA?) and got back calibrated probabilities rather than a flat 1.0/0.0 — Jev and OpenAI's model are text/JSON-only, so Gemini's is the only one of the three that handles images, audio, video, and PDFs natively.
items.why: If part of your agent pipeline is a cheap yes/no or routing decision, this is a purpose-built, much cheaper primitive than spending a full LLM call on it — and now the only one of the three that works directly on video or a scanned PDF.
items.action: Next time you're tempted to burn a full model call on a yes/no gate or a routing decision inside an agent, check whether a decision-model API (Gemini Decision 1, GPT-6 Luna, or Jev) can do it in one pass for a fraction of the cost.

eval.reason: Concrete, hands-on technical comparison across three real decision-model APIs with his own test data, posted Nov 11, 2026; the underlying Gemini Decision 1 API was independently confirmed first-party at blog.google/innovation-and-ai/technology/developers-tools/gemini-decisions-api/ (also Nov 11, Google DeepMind). Not a duplicate — distinct from the already-sent Gemini 4 Carbon item (Nov 11) and the already-sent recursive-fast-classifier Watch Queue video (Nov 11); complementary, not overlapping.

Re-fetched simonwillison.net live this run and located the exact dated entry/permalink (/2026/Nov/11/gemini-decisions-api/, 10:03pm) via the page's own link; also independently re-fetched Google's first-party blog post.
Pricing ($0.10/M input, free output; Jev at $0.042/M), latency (150-250ms), question-type list, and his JSON test output are all quoted directly from the two fetched sources.
Not a SHIPPED item.
Clears the standing 'where do I use this' bar directly: a specific, buildable technique (swap a full LLM call for a decision-model call) with his own test data backing it, not pure discourse.

items.title: LangChain's own sales team runs a production Deep Agent — and shares the numbers, warts included
items.summary: LangChain's internal GTM Agent (built on Managed Deep Agents + LangSmith) drafts account plans, proposals, and onboarding docs from Salesforce, Drive, and call transcripts — over 100 artifacts a week for the last 12 weeks. Deals where a rep sent one of its documents progressed to a later stage 47% of the time, vs. 16% for matched deals without one (self-reported, correlational, no stated methodology); one latency fix took a run from 18 minutes down to 7. The team's own honest takeaway: most of the quality gain came from feeding the agent real business context, not from tuning the prompt.
items.why: The actual lesson here isn't the sales use case — it's that a context-engineering fix, not a prompt-engineering one, cut a production agent's runtime by more than half.
items.action: Before reaching for prompt tweaks on a slow or inconsistent agent step, check whether it's missing business/domain context the way LangChain's was — that's the fix that actually worked for them.

eval.reason: First-party, real internal production deployment (LangChain's own sales team, not a hypothetical), dated Nov 10, 2026, with several specific adoption/impact figures per the standing LangChain-impact instruction; not a duplicate of the Workday case study already sent Nov 11.
Re-fetched langchain.com/blog/gtm-agent-high-quality-sales-artifacts live this run; author (Nick Bray) and date confirmed.

47% vs 16% stage-progression figure, 46% follow-up-call rate, 1,540 artifacts/12 weeks, 337 hours saved, and the 18-to-7-minute latency fix are all quoted directly from the re-fetched post; the correlational/no-stated-methodology caveat is disclosed honestly rather than smoothed over, per the stated preference for honest caveats.
Not a SHIPPED item.

The underlying use case (sales artifacts) is outside Vikas's core stack, but the generalizable lesson — a context fix, not a prompt fix, halved a production agent's runtime — is directly applicable to harness/agent work; this trade-off is stated plainly rather than oversold.

items.title: How to Catch Edge Cases Before Your Coding Agent Writes Code — Superlinear adapts Poteto's /statechart skill
items.summary: Superlinear (a small podcast on getting more out of coding agents) walks through adapting Lauren "Poteto" Tan's /statechart skill into a workflow that models proposed behavior, lists promises, and runs a checker to surface edge cases — like duplicate jobs from retries — before an agent writes any code. A real calendar-flow example forces a rethink of the promise itself, not just the implementation; the channel's own pinned comment is upfront that verifying the model doesn't prove the eventual code matches it.
items.why: This is a concrete, honest technique for catching the kind of retry/race-condition edge case that's easy to hand-wave in a spec and easy for a coding agent to miss entirely.
items.action: 39 minutes. Note: published Nov 5 — older than usual for this slot, because today's YouTube homepage, channel pages, and search results all failed to render (a harder failure than the usual logged-out fallback); judged via the full description, chapter list, and comments rather than a transcript, since the transcript panel couldn't be opened this run either.

eval.reason: Substantive technical walkthrough (adapting a known creator's skill, real example, honest Q&A on limitations), not hype; not a duplicate of anything previously sent.
